item.title: Ollama: Local LLM Inference for Personal Computers and Small Services
item.description:
Ollama packages model acquisition, local inference, a command-line interface, a desktop application, and an HTTP API into one tool. It is one of the easiest ways to download an open-weight model and run it on a developer workstation without first assembling a Python environment, inference engine, tokenizer, prompt template, and GPU runtime.

A minimal session is:

sh 
ollama pull qwen3:8b
ollama run qwen3:8b

Ollama selects an appropriate local runner, stores the model, starts it when needed, and applies the model’s chat template. This convenience makes Ollama a good fit for personal computers, application development, demonstrations, and small internal services. It does not automatically make a laptop into a high-throughput or highly available production inference cluster.

item.title: Background Detection, Blur, and Removal
item.description: Replacing a background sounds like one operation, but it is a pipeline of different problems. A system must decide what the foreground is, estimate how strongly each pixel belongs to it, apply an effect, and composite the result. The best algorithm therefore depends less on a leaderboard than on the input, the amount of user guidance, the hardware, and whether the output is a photograph or an unending live stream.

item.title: What Happens After You Send a Message in an LLM Chat UI
item.description:
A chat interface makes an interaction with a large language model look simple: type a message, press Enter, and watch an answer appear. Behind that interaction is a distributed request pipeline involving the browser, application servers, databases, policy systems, model gateways, inference workers, and often tools or retrieval services.

In an existing conversation, the new text is only one part of the model’s input. The application must reconstruct enough of the conversation, combine it with hidden instructions and other context, fit everything into a finite context window, run inference, stream the result, and persist the new state.

item.title: RAG, GraphRAG, and LLM Wikis: Three Ways to Give AI Access to Knowledge
item.description:
A large language model knows only what its training and current context make available. It does not automatically know a company’s latest policies, a customer’s current order status, or the contents of a private document repository.

Three related approaches try to close that gap:

  1. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) finds relevant source passages when a question is asked.
  2. GraphRAG adds an explicit model of entities, relationships, and larger themes.
  3. An LLM wiki uses an LLM to incrementally compile source material into a persistent, navigable wiki.

These terms are often mixed together, but they solve different problems. RAG is primarily a retrieval pattern. GraphRAG is a family of graph-assisted retrieval patterns. “LLM wiki” is an emerging design pattern, not an established industry standard.

item.title: Spark Structured Streaming
item.description:
Spark Structured Streaming is the stream-processing layer of Apache Spark. It represents an unbounded input stream as an incrementally updated table, lets an application describe the computation with the DataFrame or Dataset API, and repeatedly executes that computation as new records arrive.

Structured Streaming is not a separate cluster service. A streaming query runs inside a normal Spark application: the driver plans and coordinates the query, executors run tasks, and a cluster manager such as Kubernetes, YARN, or Spark Standalone supplies resources. The application remains alive while one or more streaming queries are active.

item.title: Big Data File Formats
item.description:
Big-data file formats trade off storage efficiency, schema evolution, and query speed. The best choice depends on whether the workload mostly scans records, reads a few columns across many rows, or exchanges events between systems.

Row-Oriented Formats #

Row-oriented formats place the fields of one record together. Avro is a common example. It is useful for streaming, event interchange, and write-heavy workloads because reading a complete record is efficient. Avro stores its writer schema with the data and has explicit schema-resolution rules that support compatible evolution.

item.title: Spark ML
item.description:
Spark includes a machine-learning library named MLlib. The phrase “Spark ML” is commonly used for MLlib’s DataFrame-based API because its Java and Scala classes live under org.apache.spark.ml and its Python classes under pyspark.ml.

These names are easy to confuse:

Name Meaning
MLlib Spark’s complete machine-learning library
spark.ml The primary, DataFrame-based MLlib API
spark.mllib The older RDD-based API, now in maintenance mode
Spark ML An informal name for the spark.ml API

spark.mllib is not removed, but new application code should normally use spark.ml. The DataFrame API integrates with Spark SQL, has a consistent pipeline model, and provides similar APIs across Java, Scala, and Python.

item.title: Introduction to Apache Kyuubi
item.description:
Apache Kyuubi is a multi-tenant SQL gateway for distributed data systems. It gives people and BI tools a stable JDBC or ODBC endpoint without requiring every user to manage Spark application lifecycles, cluster queues, or engine configuration.

Kyuubi separates a long-lived client endpoint from the processes that execute queries. This distinction is its main architectural contribution:

  • Kyuubi servers authenticate clients, maintain protocol sessions, select engines, and forward operations.
  • Kyuubi engines run SQL and consume compute resources. Spark SQL is the most common engine, while Kyuubi releases can also integrate with other query engines.
  • External services still provide resource management, metadata, storage, authorization policy, and service discovery.

Kyuubi therefore does not replace Spark, YARN, Kubernetes, a Hive metastore, or object storage. It coordinates access to them.

item.title: Apache Hive / Kyuubi Overview
item.description:
Apache Hive provides SQL semantics over datasets stored in distributed filesystems and object stores. A Hive deployment is not one daemon or one storage format. It combines a SQL language, metadata services, query compilation, an execution engine, warehouse storage, and client protocols.

Several names surrounding Hive refer to different layers:

  1. Hive is the project, HiveQL language, compiler, optimizer, runtime integration, and supporting services.
  2. Hive Metastore (HMS) stores and serves table, partition, schema, location, statistics, and transaction metadata. HMS stores metadata rather than table data.
  3. HiveServer2 (HS2) accepts remote JDBC and ODBC sessions, compiles HiveQL, coordinates execution, and returns results.
  4. hive CLI is the historical thick command-line client. It loads Hive runtime code locally and should not be confused with HiveServer2.
  5. Beeline is a JDBC command-line client. Shared deployments use Beeline against HiveServer2 because authentication, configuration, auditing, and resource control remain on the server.
  6. Apache Kyuubi is a multi-tenant SQL gateway with a HiveServer2-compatible protocol. It can manage engines such as Spark SQL, but Kyuubi is not HiveServer2 and does not turn Spark SQL into the Hive execution engine.
  7. Kerberos authenticates users and services across Hadoop components. Kerberos does not define table schemas, execute SQL, or decide SQL privileges.
  8. Apache Kite SDK belongs to the historical Hadoop dataset-tooling ecosystem. It is not part of a current Hive query path.

The distinctions matter because a JDBC connection can succeed while HMS is unavailable, an HMS lookup can succeed while HDFS permissions reject a query, and a Kyuubi endpoint can speak the HiveServer2 protocol without executing Hive’s compiler or runtime.

item.title: Docker-based Hadoop/Spark/Hive Orchestration
item.description:
Hadoop, Spark, and Hive have overlapping Java, Hadoop-client, and configuration requirements. Installing every distribution on a workstation also mixes cluster state with host files. A Docker Compose lab avoids both problems by mounting an immutable software tree at /opt/ro and placing daemon state in named volumes.

The guide builds the lab in five stages:

  1. Start an offline toolbox with the JDK, Hadoop, Hive, and Spark commands but no cluster daemons.
  2. Add one HDFS NameNode and three DataNodes.
  3. Add one YARN ResourceManager and three NodeManagers.
  4. Add HiveServer2 with an embedded Derby metastore.
  5. Run Spark locally and on YARN.

Scope and Architecture #

The lab runs all roles on one Docker host:

item.title: Apache Polaris and Apache Iceberg
item.description:
Apache Polaris is a catalog service for Apache Iceberg tables. Apache Iceberg is an open table format for large analytical datasets. Neither project is a general-purpose computation engine:

  • Polaris identifies tables, governs access, and coordinates changes to the current Iceberg metadata.
  • Iceberg defines how table state, snapshots, manifests, data files, and delete files fit together.
  • Spark, Flink, Trino, and other engines plan and execute computations.
  • HDFS or object storage holds the Iceberg metadata and table data files.

Keeping those responsibilities separate prevents a common category error: Polaris is not an alternative to Spark. A Spark deployment can use Polaris as its Iceberg catalog.

item.title: Apache Kafka
item.description:
Apache Kafka is a distributed append-log system for durable event streams. Producers append records to topic partitions, brokers replicate and retain those records, and consumers read them by offset. Kafka is therefore useful when several independent applications need to observe the same ordered history without coupling their availability or processing rate.

Cluster Roles and Metadata #

A Kafka cluster contains two server roles:

  • Brokers store partition replicas and serve produce and fetch requests.
  • KRaft controllers maintain cluster metadata, broker membership, topic configuration, replica placement, and partition leadership.

A process can perform one or both roles in a development cluster. Production clusters separate controller and broker roles because data-plane load should not interfere with metadata quorum decisions. ZooKeeper belongs to Kafka’s legacy metadata architecture and is absent from Kafka 4.x.

item.title: Apache Flink and Kafka Integration
item.description:
Apache Flink is a distributed processing engine for stateful computations over bounded and unbounded data streams. It can consume events as they arrive, maintain application state, use event time, recover from failures, and continuously publish results.

Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform. Producers append records to partitioned topics, Kafka retains those records, and consumers read them at their own pace. Kafka is commonly the durable transport layer in a streaming architecture, while Flink performs the computation:

item.title: Apache Spark
item.description:
Spark application is just a type of yarn application.

Apache Spark is written in Scala and runs on any JVM as long as compatible scala runtime jars are presented on classpath.

A worker node requires HDFS and YARN client to work, and read / write files on a HDFS for job input and output.

Overview #

The user write a JVM bytecode program (either in Java or Scala), known as the driver program, and package into a foo.jar jar file. This jar file may include all dependencies (a.k.a a uber jar), or lack them in expectation of they are provided by worker node environment.

item.title: Hadoop Overview
item.description:
Apache Hadoop is a Java framework for storing data across a cluster and executing distributed applications near that data. Its original batch model combines three separate responsibilities:

  1. HDFS stores one logical filesystem across machines.
  2. YARN allocates cluster resources and launches application processes.
  3. MapReduce divides a batch computation into map, shuffle, and reduce phases.

Hadoop Common supplies the configuration, filesystem abstractions, security support, native-library integration, and command launchers used by those projects. Separating the responsibilities matters because HDFS can store data for applications other than MapReduce, and YARN can schedule application frameworks other than MapReduce.

item.title: LangGraph4j
item.description:
LangGraph4j is a Java library for building stateful, graph-based AI applications. A graph consists of nodes that perform work, edges that select the next node, and shared state that changes as the graph runs. It is inspired by LangGraph and integrates with LangChain4j and Spring AI, but a graph node can also be ordinary Java code.

text 
 +------------+
 | call model |
 +------+-----+
 |
 tool requested?
 / \
 yes no
 / \
 +-------v-------+ +--v--+
 | execute tool | | END |
 +-------+-------+ +-----+
 |
 +----------> call model

Cycles are intentional. They let an application reason, act, inspect a result, and reason again. LangGraph4j makes that control flow and its state explicit; it also provides reducers, conditional routing, checkpoints, breakpoints, streaming, graph visualization, and subgraphs.

item.title: The A2A Protocol
item.description:
inventing mcp again.

The Agent2Agent Protocol, abbreviated A2A, is an open protocol for communication between independent AI-agent applications. It lets one agent discover another agent’s capabilities, send it work, continue a multi-turn interaction, track a long-running task, and receive structured results without knowing how the remote agent is implemented.

A2A was initiated by Google and donated to the Linux Foundation. It is framework-, model-, language-, and vendor-neutral. An A2A client built in Java can collaborate with a remote agent built in Python using a different model and agent framework.

item.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.description:
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, retrieves information from an external corpus and supplies selected evidence to a generative model for one request.

A minimal RAG system has two paths:

text 
Indexing path

documents -> parse -> normalize -> split -> embed -> index

Request path

question -> retrieve -> rank -> select context -> generate -> answer

RAG does not modify the language model’s parameters. It changes the input context presented to the model. This makes it useful for information that is:

item.title: Hugging Face Transformer Repositories
item.description:
The Hugging Face transformers library provides model implementations, preprocessing utilities, training integrations, and convenient loading APIs for pretrained models. A compatible model repository is a versioned collection of model artifacts and configuration files that lets the library reconstruct the model and its inputs.

Repository Contents #

A typical repository contains a model configuration such as config.json, weights in a supported format such as model.safetensors, and preprocessing artifacts. Text models commonly include tokenizer files; vision, audio, and multimodal models may include image, feature-extractor, processor, or generation configuration files.

item.title: OpenAI Chat Completions and Spring AI
item.description:
The OpenAI Chat Completions API is a widely implemented JSON-over-HTTP interface for conversational language models. A client sends an ordered list of messages and generation options; the server returns one or more assistant messages with metadata and token usage.

Its basic shape is:

text 
HTTP client
 -> POST /v1/chat/completions
 -> request JSON containing messages and options
 -> model inference
 <- response JSON containing choices and usage

Many gateways and model servers implement an OpenAI-compatible endpoint even when the underlying model is not hosted by OpenAI. This makes the format a useful de facto interoperability API, but it is not an independent formal standard like HTTP, JSON-RPC, or MCP. Compatible providers may support different fields, models, limits, error formats, or extensions.

item.title: Recommender Systems
item.description:
A recommender system ranks items a person may find useful by learning from product interactions and item information. Its output may drive search suggestions, home-page ranking, notification selection, or merchandising rather than a single “you may also like” widget.

Collaborative Filtering #

Collaborative filtering recommends items using patterns across users and items. An interaction can be an explicit rating or an implicit signal such as a click, watch time, purchase, save, or skip. For \(n\) users and \(m\) items, the observations can be represented as a sparse \(n \times m\) interaction matrix.

item.title: Machine Learning Optimizers
item.description:
An optimizer updates model parameters to reduce a training objective. In gradient-based learning, the objective measures the mismatch between predictions and targets, and automatic differentiation supplies gradients with respect to the parameters.

Gradient Descent #

For parameters \(\theta\), learning rate \(\eta\), and loss \(L\), gradient descent performs:

text 
θ ← θ − η ∇θL

Batch gradient descent uses the entire training set for each update. Stochastic gradient descent uses one example, and mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch. Mini-batches are the standard practical choice because they use accelerator hardware efficiently while adding gradient noise that can help exploration.

item.title: Machine Learning Engineering Overview
item.description:
Machine learning engineering connects experimentation to dependable systems. It includes data contracts, reproducible training, evaluation, packaging, deployment, monitoring, and iteration—not only selecting a model architecture.

The Scientific Python Foundation #

NumPy provides the core multidimensional array type and numerical operations. SciPy builds on NumPy with algorithms for optimization, statistics, signal processing, and scientific computing. Scikit-learn provides accessible implementations of classical machine-learning models, preprocessing, model selection, and evaluation tools.

sh 
python -m pip install numpy scipy scikit-learn

Use virtual environments and lock dependency versions for repeatable work. NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn are separate projects with complementary scopes.

item.title: Classification Models and Learning Objectives
item.description:
Statistical learning assumes that training examples provide evidence about the population on which a model will operate. Sampling bias, label error, and distribution shift can invalidate that assumption; a high validation score then does not establish production performance.

Linear Scores and Logistic Regression #

A linear model computes a score \(z = w^\mathsf{T}x + b\). Linear regression predicts a continuous target, so thresholding its output does not make it a probabilistic classifier.

item.title: Torch and PyTorch
item.description:
Torch was an early machine-learning framework with a Lua interface and a C/CUDA core. PyTorch is its successor ecosystem: it retains the name and some implementation heritage, but it is an actively developed framework centered on Python and C++ APIs. LibTorch is PyTorch’s C++ distribution.

Install PyTorch #

For most Python projects, install the published package using the command generated by the PyTorch installation selector. The appropriate package depends on the operating system, Python version, and whether the application uses CPU, CUDA, or another accelerator backend.

item.title: Mem0
item.description:
Mem0 is a memory layer for AI applications. It extracts facts from interactions, reconciles those facts with existing memories, and retrieves selected memories for later prompts.

For example, an assistant may receive these statements over time:

text 
I drink dark-roast coffee without sugar.
I have switched to decaf.

A transcript store preserves both statements as events. A memory system may instead retain a current fact such as “The user drinks decaffeinated dark-roast coffee without sugar.” Mem0 packages the model calls, storage, and retrieval needed for that process.

item.title: AgentScope
item.description:
AgentScope is an open-source framework for building and operating applications in which a large language model can reason, call tools, retain state, and collaborate with users or other agents. It was initiated by Alibaba and is available as separate Python and Java projects.

An ordinary model call has a short, application-controlled path:

text 
application -> prompt -> model -> response

An agent adds an execution loop:

text 
user goal
 |
 v
model reasons -> chooses a tool -> application executes it
 ^ |
 +----------- tool result <---------+
 |
 v
final answer, interruption, or next action

The model still does not execute Java or Python functions by itself. It emits a structured request, and AgentScope validates and dispatches that request through its tool system. The framework also manages the messages, event stream, permissions, session state, and repeated model calls around that loop.

item.title: Spring AI
item.description:
Spring AI is a Spring project for building applications that use generative-AI models. It provides portable Java interfaces for model access and Spring Boot auto-configuration for model providers, vector stores, tool calling, conversation memory, retrieval augmented generation, observability, evaluation, and the Model Context Protocol.

Spring AI does not contain a language model. It connects an application to a remote or local model:

text 
Spring application
 -> Spring AI ChatClient / model API
 -> provider SDK or HTTP API
 -> OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Amazon, Azure, Ollama, or another provider

Its role is similar to Spring Data’s role for databases: application code uses common concepts while provider adapters handle transport and provider-specific details. The abstraction reduces coupling, but providers are not identical. Model names, token limits, structured-output behavior, tool support, safety controls, and request options still vary.

item.title: Vector Stores
item.description:
A vector store stores numeric vectors and retrieves the items whose vectors are nearest to a query vector. In AI applications, those vectors are commonly embeddings: compact numeric representations of text, images, audio, users, products, or other objects.

Vector stores make questions such as these practical:

  • Which documentation passages are semantically related to this question?
  • Which products resemble the one a customer is viewing?
  • Have we processed a support ticket with the same meaning before?
  • Which tools are relevant to the user’s current goal?
  • Which saved memories may matter in this conversation?

A vector store is not a language model, and it does not generate an answer. It is a retrieval component. It finds candidate data; application code or a model then decides how to use that data.

item.title: Model Context Protocol
item.description:
MCP just say that: here is a jsonrpc-based schema, please follow this for the http request-response if the communication parties happened to be an LLM-using program (agent) and an arbitrary http server that is meant to provide arbitrary abilities.

Model Context Protocol, usually abbreviated as MCP, is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and contextual data. It gives an AI host one consistent way to discover and invoke capabilities provided by local programs, remote services, databases, and other systems.

item.title: Word Embeddings and A La Carte Embeddings
item.description:
Word embeddings map words to vectors so that a model can work with language numerically. A useful embedding places words used in similar contexts near one another: vectors for cat and dog, for example, should usually be more similar than vectors for cat and database. Similarity is commonly measured with cosine similarity.

How Distributional Embeddings Work #

The distributional hypothesis is the practical idea behind many embeddings: words that occur in similar contexts tend to have related meanings. Algorithms such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and fastText learn vector representations from large text collections by predicting nearby words or by factoring word-context statistics.

item.title: NVIDIA Triton Inference Server
item.description:
NVIDIA Triton Inference Server serves machine-learning models over HTTP and gRPC. It supports several backends, including TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, TensorFlow, Python, and ensembles, while providing batching, metrics, model versioning, and concurrency controls.

Start with a Container #

The supported Triton containers are published through NVIDIA NGC:

sh 
docker pull nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:<tag>
docker run --gpus all --rm -p 8000:8000 -p 8001:8001 \
 -v "$PWD/models:/models" \
 nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:<tag> tritonserver \
 --model-repository=/models

Select a tag whose backend support matches the model. Minimal images contain the server only, while other images add selected framework or SDK components. Check the release notes for compatibility among the server, CUDA driver, and model runtime.

item.title: Linear Algebra Essentials
item.description:
Linear algebra describes vectors, matrices, and transformations between vector spaces. It is central to machine learning because data, parameters, embeddings, and many model operations are represented as arrays of numbers.

Vectors and Linear Combinations #

A vector is an ordered collection of scalars. Given vectors \(v_1, \ldots, v_n\) and scalars \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\), their linear combination is:

text 
a₁v₁ + a₂v₂ + ... + aₙvₙ

The span of a set of vectors is the set of every linear combination of those vectors. A set spans a vector space when every vector in that space can be expressed using it.

item.title: Probability and Distributions
item.description:
Probability describes uncertainty under a model. It does not establish causation: correlated variables can have a strong conditional relationship without either causing the other.

Random Variables and Moments #

A random variable maps outcomes to values. Its distribution assigns probability mass or density to those values. For a scalar random variable \(X\), expectation and variance are:

\[ \mathbb{E}[X], \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2]. \]

Standard deviation is the square root of variance. For a random vector \(X\), the mean is a vector and covariance is a matrix:

item.description:
InnoDB transactions protect database invariants by committing related changes atomically and controlling how concurrent statements observe them. Isolation is not a replacement for constraints: use primary, unique, foreign-key, and check constraints for invariants the schema can express, then select a transaction and locking pattern for multi-statement decisions.

Transaction Boundaries and Autocommit #

item.title: Redis Caching and Coordination Patterns
item.description:
Redis is an in-memory data-structure server that can accelerate reads and coordinate bounded operations. A production design must define the source of truth, consistency window, capacity policy, failure behavior, and ownership of every key. Persistence and replication improve recovery options; they do not give a cache the transactional invariants of its source database.

Cache-Aside and Consistency Windows #

Cache-aside leaves read and write policy in the application:

The application reads Redis, loads a miss from the database, stores the result with a TTL, and returns it. A source write must invalidate or refresh affected keys. Because database commit and cache mutation are not one atomic operation, readers can observe stale data between those events. Define the acceptable window and use a transactional outbox or change-data stream when cache invalidation must survive process failure.

item.title: Cryptography Foundations
item.description: Cryptography applies mathematical primitives to security goals such as confidentiality, integrity, peer authentication, and non-repudiation. A secure primitive does not make a protocol secure by itself because encodings, key management, randomness, state, and the attacker’s capabilities also determine the result.

item.title: Linux Kernel Network Feature Timeline
item.description:
Linux networking evolves through incremental mainline releases rather than separate subsystem releases. The milestones below identify the first stable kernel containing each feature; later kernels may add protocol coverage, drivers, offloads, or userspace interfaces.

Network Feature Quick Facts #

Feature Kernel Release Date Maintainer Page Quick Fact
Netfilter and iptables 2.4.0 January 4, 2001 netfilter.org Netfilter introduced extensible packet-processing hooks, while iptables exposed filtering, NAT, and packet-mangling rules to userspace.
NAPI 2.6.0 December 17, 2003 NAPI combined interrupt notification with polling, thus reducing interrupt overhead when interfaces receive packets at high rates.
CUBIC TCP congestion control 2.6.13 August 28, 2005 CUBIC selects the congestion window from a cubic function of time since the previous congestion event. Linux 2.6.19 later made it the default TCP congestion-control algorithm.
Network namespaces 2.6.24 January 24, 2008 Initial support isolated network devices, protocol stacks, routing tables, firewall rules, and sockets. Subsequent releases expanded device and protocol coverage.
Generic Receive Offload (GRO) 2.6.29 March 23, 2009 GRO aggregates related packets before upper-layer processing, thus amortizing per-packet costs without requiring NIC-specific receive offload.
Receive Packet Steering and Receive Flow Steering 2.6.35 August 1, 2010 RPS distributes receive processing across CPUs in software, while RFS adds flow locality so packet processing can follow the consuming application.
TCP Fast Open client support 3.6 September 30, 2012 TFO can carry application data in the opening SYN when the client has a valid cookie. Server support followed in Linux 3.7.
nftables 3.13 January 20, 2014 nftables project nftables added a programmable packet-classification engine and a Netlink API intended to replace the separate iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables interfaces.
Extended BPF 3.18 December 7, 2014 eBPF project The bpf() system call and eBPF virtual machine provided the foundation for verified, JIT-compiled programs used by socket filters, traffic control, tracing, and later XDP.
Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) 4.3 November 2, 2015 The VRF device lets interfaces share a network namespace while using separate routing tables, which supports route isolation without creating another namespace.
eXpress Data Path (XDP) 4.8 October 2, 2016 XDP project XDP runs eBPF programs before the kernel allocates a socket buffer, enabling early packet drop, redirection, and load balancing.
BBR congestion control 4.9 December 11, 2016 Google BBR BBR models bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time instead of treating packet loss as the primary congestion signal.
Kernel TLS transmit offload 4.13 September 3, 2017 kTLS moved TLS record encryption and framing for transmitted data into the kernel. Receive support followed in Linux 4.17.
AF_XDP sockets 4.18 August 12, 2018 XDP project AF_XDP connects XDP programs to userspace through shared-memory rings, supporting copy and zero-copy operation depending on the driver.
Multipath TCP 5.6 March 29, 2020 MPTCP upstream project Initial upstream MPTCP support allowed one logical transport connection to use multiple TCP subflows across different paths.
WireGuard 5.6 March 29, 2020 WireGuard WireGuard added an in-kernel encrypted layer-3 tunnel with a small protocol and cryptographic surface.
IPv6 BIG TCP 5.19 July 31, 2022 BIG TCP allows larger non-GSO packet sizes inside the host stack, thus reducing per-packet overhead on high-speed links. IPv4 support followed in Linux 6.3.

Release dates follow the mainline tags in the Linux kernel Git history. Feature versions are cross-referenced with the KernelNewbies release summaries and the kernel networking documentation.

item.title: iproute2
item.description:
iproute2 is the standard Linux userspace suite for inspecting and configuring the kernel networking stack. The suite covers links, addresses, routes, neighbours, tunnels, traffic control, sockets, hardware offload, and several specialized networking subsystems. Most commands exchange Netlink messages with the kernel; they do not implement the data plane that forwards packets.

The project publishes one release for each Linux kernel release. Matching versions expose the same generation of kernel interfaces, although a newer iproute2 can operate against an older kernel when it does not request unsupported features.

item.title: Automatic Speech Recognition: From Hidden Markov Models to Speech Foundation Models
item.description: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) converts a speech waveform into text. A production transcription system also has to decide when speech begins and ends, identify the language, place timestamps, separate speakers, restore punctuation, adapt to domain vocabulary, and deliver results within a latency and compute budget.

item.title: Linux Packet Filtering with iptables and nftables
item.description:
Linux packet filtering is implemented by Netfilter, a kernel framework that exposes hooks in the networking stack. iptables and nftables are not independent firewalls: they are userspace interfaces for programming packet classification and actions at those hooks.

iptables is the historical interface. Native nftables, configured with the nft command, replaces the separate iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables rule-management models with one language and one Netlink API. Compatibility tools can still accept iptables syntax while writing to the nftables kernel backend, so the command name alone does not identify the active implementation.

item.title: LXC and Linux System Containers
item.description:
LXC is a userspace interface for Linux containment features. It combines the liblxc library, command-line tools, and distribution templates to create system containers: isolated Linux userspaces that share the host’s kernel.

An LXC container can boot an init system, run several services, maintain persistent package state, and expose virtual network interfaces. The operating model therefore resembles a lightweight Linux machine more than an OCI application container. LXC remains a container runtime, however, because it does not boot a guest kernel or emulate hardware.

item.title: Object Detection Algorithms
item.description: Object detection answers two questions: what objects are present, and where are they? A detector normally returns a set of class labels, confidence scores, and bounding boxes. Over several decades, the field has moved from hand-built templates scanned across an image to neural networks that predict many objects in one pass, and then to transformers and vision-language models that can search for categories described in text.

item.description:

Its core API does not depend on JUnit: a program can create a mock, configure behavior, invoke code, and verify interactions from an ordinary main method. JUnit integration adds test discovery and automatic mock lifecycle management rather than basic mocking capability.

import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;

}

public final class MockitoHello {
 public static void main(String[] args) {
 Greeter greeter = mock(Greeter.class);
 when(greeter.greet("Ada")).thenReturn("Hello, Ada");

item.title: Testing Spring Boot REST APIs
item.description:
Testing a Spring Boot REST API requires several scopes because a direct Java call, a simulated MVC request, and a request through a live server exercise different failure boundaries. A useful test suite places most behavior checks below the Spring context, then adds narrower web slices and a smaller number of full-application tests.

item.title: Kerberos
item.description:
Kerberos is a network authentication protocol for systems under coordinated administration. A user authenticates to a trusted Key Distribution Center (KDC), then obtains time-limited tickets for individual services. Services can verify the user’s identity without receiving the user’s password, and clients can request proof that a service possesses the expected secret.

Kerberos primarily uses symmetric cryptography. Symmetric cryptography makes the KDC a central trust anchor: compromise of a KDC or its database can compromise every principal whose long-term key the KDC controls. Kerberos therefore trades decentralized trust for centralized identity administration, efficient ticket issuance, and single-sign-on within a realm.

item.title: Research Unix History
item.description:
Unix began as a small Bell Labs system and became several related things: a source- code lineage, an interface tradition, a standardized environment, and a registered trademark. Historical claims become misleading when those categories are collapsed into one family tree.

From Multics to the PDP-7 #

Bell Labs participated with MIT and General Electric in the Multics project during the 1960s, then withdrew in 1969. Ken Thompson retained an interest in interactive computing and filesystem design. He had also written Space Travel, first for Multics and then for a GECOS system whose development cycle made experimentation expensive.

item.title: Linux Networking
item.description:
Linux exposes network state through namespace-aware interfaces. Since Linux 2.6.25, /proc/net is a compatibility symlink to /proc/self/net, so it describes the network namespace of the reading process. Modern tools normally use Netlink instead of parsing procfs.

Routes and Netlink #

The IPv4 Forwarding Information Base (FIB) determines where packets are sent. /proc/net/route is a historical view of it; ip route queries and changes the kernel through Netlink. Netlink is a family of message-oriented sockets that lets userspace configure and inspect kernel subsystems without adding a new syscall. Routing, links, addresses, neighbours, traffic control, and Netfilter all use it.

item.title: Linux eBPF
item.description:
eBPF is a verified execution environment in the Linux kernel. Applications load programs and maps, attach programs to kernel-defined hooks, and exchange data through file descriptors. Networking remains an important use, but tracing, security policy, and performance analysis no longer depend on packet capture.

From Packet Filters to Linux Socket Filters #

The design lineage begins with DEC’s packet filter for systems including ULTRIX and DIGITAL UNIX. A process opened a packet-filter device, selected an interface, installed an enfilter instruction sequence with ioctl(), and read accepted link-layer packets. The filter used a stack machine, and multiple consumers were ordered by priority.

item.title: GNU Bison
item.description:
GNU Bison generates parsers from context-free grammars. Its Yacc-compatible notation defines tokens, nonterminals, semantic values, and actions; the generated parser obtains tokens from a scanner by convention. Consult the GNU Bison manual for skeleton- and language-specific interfaces.

Grammar Sections, Values, and Actions #

A grammar has declarations, productions, and optional epilogue code, separated by %%. Declarations define tokens, value types, precedence, parser settings, and required code. Productions define nonterminals and actions.

item.title: Using Thymeleaf without Spring MVC
item.description:
Thymeleaf can render HTML in a batch job, command-line program, mail service, or report pipeline without Spring MVC. A standalone application configures a template resolver and TemplateEngine, supplies a context, and writes the rendered output to its destination.

item.title: Git Line-Ending Conversion
item.description:
Git can normalize text to LF at the repository boundary while presenting LF or CRLF in a worktree. A stable .gitattributes policy avoids platform-dependent commits and leaves editors responsible only for the checked-out form.

Distinguish HEAD, Index, and Worktree Bytes #

A tracked path has three relevant representations:

  1. HEAD names the blob stored by the current commit.
  2. The index holds the blob proposed for the next commit.
  3. The worktree holds bytes consumed by editors and build tools.

For normalized text, git add performs a clean conversion from CRLF to LF. Checkout performs a smudge conversion from indexed LF to the selected worktree ending. Existing commits are not rewritten.

item.title: C++ Containers and Iterators
item.description:
Choose a container from the required lookup, traversal, insertion, erasure, memory locality, and reference-stability properties. Complexity describes an operation under its preconditions; invalidation and ownership determine whether a design remains correct after mutation.

Selecting a Container #

  • std::vector is the default sequence for contiguous storage, random access, cache locality, and C interoperation through data(). Appending is amortized constant time. Any capacity growth invalidates every iterator, pointer, and reference; without growth, insertion invalidates iterators and references at or after the insertion point.
  • std::deque supports indexed access. End insertion invalidates iterators but not references; its storage is non-contiguous, and middle insertion invalidates iterators and references.
  • std::list and std::forward_list retain iterators and references to unaffected nodes across insertion and erasure. Their node allocation and pointer chasing make them a measured choice, not a default.
  • std::map and std::set provide ordered traversal and logarithmic lookup. Insertion does not invalidate iterators or references, except erased elements.
  • std::unordered_map and std::unordered_set provide average constant-time lookup. Rehash invalidates iterators, although references and pointers to elements remain valid; erasing invalidates only the erased element.

reserve() avoids predicted vector reallocations and can also reduce unordered_* rehashing. It does not make an iterator valid after an operation whose documented rules invalidate it.

item.title: Jakarta Persistence, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA
item.description:
Jakarta Persistence defines the standard Java API for object-relational mapping. Hibernate is a widely used implementation. Spring Data JPA builds repository abstractions on top of a Jakarta Persistence provider.

The Jakarta Persistence Model #

An application maps ordinary classes to database tables with annotations such as @Entity, @Table, @Id, and @Column:

java 
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class PurchaseOrder {
 @Id
 @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
 private Long id;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private String status;
}

The standard APIs live in jakarta.persistence. An implementation discovers a jakarta.persistence.spi.PersistenceProvider through Java’s service-provider mechanism. The provider translates persistence operations and JPQL or Criteria queries into database-specific SQL.

item.description:
Python invocation decides both the code that executes and the first entry on sys.path. The surrounding notes cover supporting runtime concepts encountered when building tools and static sites.

Choose a Python Invocation Form #

Command Executed Entry Point Initial Import Context

-P or PYTHONSAFEPATH prevents Python from prepending the script directory or current directory. Use it in commands where importing an adjacent, untrusted file would be unsafe.

item.title: MySQL SELECT Patterns
item.description:
SELECT can read rows, combine sources, filter, aggregate, order, and limit a result. A useful outline of its syntax is:

sql 
SELECT [DISTINCT] select_expr [, ...]
FROM table_references [PARTITION (partition_names)]
WHERE condition
GROUP BY group_expr [, ...]
HAVING condition
WINDOW window_name AS (window_spec) [, ...]
ORDER BY order_expr [ASC | DESC] [, ...]
LIMIT {row_count | offset, row_count | row_count OFFSET offset};

Logical query processing provides a model for reasoning about a result:

  1. FROM, including joins, constructs candidate rows.
  2. WHERE filters individual rows.
  3. GROUP BY forms groups and aggregate functions compute group values.
  4. HAVING filters groups; named windows are then available for window functions.
  5. The select list produces output columns, DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows, ORDER BY orders them, and LIMIT restricts the returned rows.

The optimizer is free to transform and reorder physical operations when the result preserves these semantics. For example, it can push a predicate into an index access or choose a different join order. Logical processing is therefore not an execution plan; use EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to inspect the plan.

item.title: Modern Android Development
item.description:
Modern Android applications commonly use Kotlin, AndroidX, Jetpack libraries, and Jetpack Compose. Platform APIs remain in android.*; AndroidX supplies version-compatible and higher-level APIs in androidx.*. An application package has multiple system-managed entry points rather than a conventional process-wide main() method.

Application Isolation #

Android assigns an installed package a Linux UID and gives its private files UID-based ownership. An application process runs its own Android Runtime instance, and cross-package component calls use Binder IPC. Runtime permissions, SELinux, and framework service checks supplement the UID boundary.

item.title: Linux Kernel Build System
item.description:
The Linux kernel uses GNU Make and Kbuild to configure, compile, link, and install the kernel and its modules. A normal build starts with a configuration target and then builds the default target:

sh 
make defconfig
make -j"$(nproc)"

The principal result is vmlinux, an ELF executable. Architectures may additionally produce bootable wrappers such as bzImage, zImage, or vmlinuz. Loadable modules are ELF relocatable objects linked into .ko files.

item.title: Linux Kernel Source Tree
item.description:
The Linux source tree separates architecture-independent subsystems from architecture ports, public userspace interfaces, generated build state, tools, and tests. Directory names are a navigation aid rather than an execution model: Kconfig selects configuration, Kbuild selects objects, and the selected objects determine what reaches a particular kernel image.

Top-Level Subsystem Boundaries #

The principal source directories are:

Path Responsibility
arch/ Architecture ports, boot code, MMU and interrupt entry, and low-level ABI support.
block/, fs/, mm/, net/ The block layer; VFS and filesystem implementations; virtual and physical memory management; and networking stacks.
kernel/, init/, ipc/, security/ Core scheduling, locking, signals, tracing, and other kernel facilities; early initialization; IPC; and Linux Security Module infrastructure.
drivers/, sound/, virt/ Device drivers, the sound subsystem, and virtualization support such as KVM. A driver need not expose a struct file_operations; subsystem-specific buses and callbacks are also common.
crypto/, lib/, io_uring/, rust/ Shared cryptographic and library support, asynchronous I/O, and Rust kernel support.
include/, Documentation/, scripts/ Headers, maintained documentation, and Kbuild/Kconfig plus generation and maintenance utilities.
tools/, samples/, usr/ Userspace tools such as perf, example programs, and built-in initramfs generation.

Other top-level material such as certs/ and LICENSES/ supports signing, licensing, or build policy. A source checkout changes over time, so inspect its top-level README, MAINTAINERS, and Documentation/ instead of assuming every release contains the same directories.

item.title: SFINAE and Template Overload Resolution
item.description:
C++ substitutes template arguments while it forms function-template candidates. Substitution failure is not an error (SFINAE) means that an invalid dependent type or expression in the immediate context of that substitution removes that candidate; it does not make arbitrary invalid template code safe.

Candidate Formation and Immediate Context #

Overload resolution begins by forming candidates. For a function template, deduction or explicitly supplied arguments can require substitution into its function type and template parameter declarations. If that immediate declaration context is invalid, the specialization is discarded and another viable overload may be selected.

item.title: BIND 9 Authoritative and Recursive DNS
item.description:
BIND 9 runs the named name server. Its configuration determines whether it answers authoritatively, offers recursion, transfers zones, or accepts dynamic updates. Treat those roles separately because an Internet-facing authoritative server should not become an open recursive resolver.

Server Configuration #

named.conf defines global options, access-control lists, zones, and logging. A minimal authoritative configuration restricts recursion and zone transfer:

named 
acl trusted-recursors { 192.0.2.0/24; 2001:db8:1::/48; };

options {
 directory "/var/named";
 listen-on { any; };
 listen-on-v6 { any; };
 recursion no;
 allow-transfer { none; };
 minimal-responses yes;
};

zone "example.net" {
 type primary;
 file "zones/example.net";
 allow-transfer { 192.0.2.53; };
};

A recursive resolver needs recursion yes and an allow-recursion or allow-query-cache ACL limited to its clients. Never expose recursion to untrusted networks unless the deployment explicitly provides a public resolver with abuse controls.

item.title: Measuring Browser and DOM Dimensions
item.description:
Browser APIs expose several coordinate systems because a screen, browser window, viewport, document, and element answer different measurement questions. Choosing an API by name alone can therefore produce scrollbar, rounding, or scrolling errors.

Window, Screen, and Viewport Measurements #

API Measurement
window.innerWidth, innerHeight Layout viewport, including a rendered classic scrollbar
window.outerWidth, outerHeight Browser window’s outside dimensions
screen.width, screen.height Screen dimensions in CSS pixels
screen.availWidth, screen.availHeight Screen space excluding reserved operating-system areas
document.documentElement.clientWidth, clientHeight Layout viewport excluding a classic scrollbar

CSS pixels are logical units. A CSS pixel can cover multiple device pixels on a high-density display, so screen.width does not necessarily equal the panel’s physical pixel count.

item.title: Wayland Display Server
item.description:
Wayland is a display protocol designed for a local client and compositor on the same kernel. A toolkit’s Wayland backend uses libwayland-client to connect to a Unix socket, usually $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/$WAYLAND_DISPLAY such as /run/user/1000/wayland-0.

Protocol Model #

Clients and the compositor exchange typed requests and events for numbered objects such as surfaces, buffers, and input seats. XML protocol definitions generate the marshalling stubs. Clients render into shared-memory or DMA-BUF-backed buffers and submit those buffers to the compositor, which combines surfaces and controls outputs and input. A Wayland compositor therefore combines roles that were often separate in an X11 server, window manager, and compositor.

Constraints therefore replace many std::enable_if SFINAE uses with declarations that expose the intended operation set; they do not prove the semantic requirements documented by an API.

item.title: Colorful Terminal Output with Jansi
item.description:
Jansi is a Java library for generating and processing ANSI escape sequences. These sequences let a terminal display colors and styles, move the cursor, erase parts of the screen, and perform other terminal operations.

For example, the following bytes mean “use bold red text,” print FAILED, and then restore the terminal’s default attributes:

text 
\u001B[1;31mFAILED\u001B[0m

Writing those codes by hand is difficult to read and easy to get wrong. Jansi provides a fluent Java API for constructing them and terminal-aware streams that can pass through, adapt, or remove them as appropriate.

item.title: C++ Language and Library Notes
item.description:
This bounded anthology collects language and toolchain-facing rules that do not require a separate article. Each section states the boundary that governs the feature, because similar-looking C++ spellings can have different ownership, lookup, or lifetime effects.

Resource Ownership and Optional State #

Ownership is the responsibility to release a resource at the correct time. Model it with RAII: acquire in construction, release in destruction, and make the object’s invariant hold across exceptional control flow. Prefer the Rule of Zero when members such as std::unique_ptr or std::vector already implement the resource policy. A type that directly manages a raw resource must define a coherent destructor, copy policy, move policy, and failure policy.

item.title: Git Workflows and Configuration
item.description:
Git records content and history, while configuration determines how a local installation presents, authenticates, and transforms that content. Separating repository policy from per-developer convenience avoids surprising commits.

Git reads configuration from several scopes. Later scopes override earlier values for a scalar key:

Scope Typical Location Intended Use
System /etc/gitconfig Installation-wide defaults
Global ~/.gitconfig or ~/.config/git/config Developer preferences
Local .git/config One repository
Worktree .git/config.worktree when enabled One linked worktree
Command git -c name=value ... One invocation

git config --list --show-origin --show-scope shows the source of every effective value. Query a key before changing it, because a value can be inherited from a system or global configuration:

item.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle and Prototype Scope
item.description:
Spring separates bean metadata from bean instances. A BeanDefinition describes how to create an object, while a BeanFactory applies that definition when the object is requested. An ApplicationContext adds coordinated startup, post-processing, events, resource loading, and shutdown.

What Happens During Context Refresh #

AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() prepares the environment and bean factory before application singletons become usable. The major stages are:

  1. Prepare or obtain the BeanFactory and load bean definitions.
  2. Invoke BeanFactoryPostProcessors, including configuration-class processing, while definitions can still be changed.
  3. Discover and register BeanPostProcessors.
  4. Initialize context infrastructure such as message resolution, events, and context-specific resources.
  5. Instantiate the remaining non-lazy singleton beans.
  6. Publish the refreshed state and ContextRefreshedEvent.

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor changes metadata. A BeanPostProcessor instead sees instances and can inject fields, invoke lifecycle annotations, or replace a bean with a proxy. Creating ordinary application beans from a factory post-processor is unsafe because it can instantiate them before all post-processors are registered.

item.title: Linux x86 Calling Conventions
item.description:
A calling convention is a binary contract for argument placement, results, preserved state, and stack layout. Linux x86-64 programs use the System V AMD64 function ABI; 32-bit programs use the System V i386 ABI. Linux system calls use separate entry ABIs and must not be treated as ordinary function calls.

AMD64 Function Calls #

The AMD64 ABI first classifies each argument. Integer-class values, including ordinary integers and pointers, use rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, and r9. SSE-class values use xmm0 through xmm7. Exhausting one class does not by itself exhaust the other; arguments that cannot be assigned according to the classification rules go in the stack input area.

item.title: Formal Languages and Parsing
item.description:
A formal language is a set of finite strings over an alphabet. A grammar defines productions that derive strings in that set. Compiler front ends use this model to separate local token recognition from recursive program structure.

Chomsky Families #

The Chomsky hierarchy classifies grammars by production restrictions:

  1. Type 3, regular grammars, describe regular languages recognized by finite automata. Regular expressions and lexers operate here.
  2. Type 2, context-free grammars (CFGs), have one nonterminal on the left of each production and are recognized by pushdown automata.
  3. Type 1, context-sensitive grammars, restrict productions so they do not shorten sentential forms except for defined start-symbol cases.
  4. Type 0, unrestricted grammars, impose no comparable production restriction.

Balanced delimiters illustrate the boundary. A finite automaton cannot remember an unbounded nesting depth, whereas a CFG can use recursion such as Group → '(' Group ')' Group | ε.

item.title: Maven
item.description:
Maven builds a project by executing plugin goals in lifecycle order. A lifecycle contains ordered phases; invoking a phase executes that phase and every earlier phase in the same lifecycle. Plugins contribute goals, and lifecycle bindings select the goals that run for a project packaging.

Project Model and Coordinates #

item.title: Git Credential Management
item.description:
Git delegates HTTP(S) authentication to credential helpers. SSH remotes use SSH keys and agents instead, so credential.helper does not manage their private keys.

Select a Credential Helper #

List configured helpers together with the configuration file that set them:

sh 
git config --show-origin --get-all credential.helper
git help -a | grep credential-

Git asks helpers in configured order to fill missing credential fields. A helper can decline or return partial data, after which Git may query another helper or prompt the user.

item.title: Spring Annotation Processing
item.description:
Spring uses annotations as declarative metadata for component discovery, configuration, dependency injection, transactions, web request mapping, and other framework services. Java reflection exposes the raw annotations; Spring adds a consistent model for composed annotations, aliases, search strategies, and metadata reading without loading classes.

Java Annotation Semantics #

An annotation declaration is itself an interface whose implicit superinterface is java.lang.annotation.Annotation:

java 
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
public @interface Audited {
}

Runtime reflection can inspect @Audited when it is directly present on a class. Meta-annotations such as @Retention, @Target, and @Documented describe an annotation declaration but do not cause arbitrary transitive lookup.

item.title: Pluggable Authentication Modules
item.description:
Linux-PAM lets an application delegate authentication policy to administrator-controlled modules. The application owns the user interaction and its privilege boundary; PAM owns a transaction handle, loads the configured stack, and combines module results. Consequently, an application can use local passwords, smart cards, directory services, MFA, or account restrictions without embedding those mechanisms.

Transaction Roles #

A PAM transaction has five roles:

  • the application starts and ends the transaction;
  • the service is the policy name supplied to pam_start, commonly login, sshd, or sudo;
  • a management group selects the operation: auth, account, session, or password;
  • a module is a shared object implementing one or more management-group entry points;
  • the conversation function lets a module request prompts, informational messages, and responses through the application.

The application begins with pam_start(service, user, &conversation, &pamh). pam_handle_t is opaque and belongs to one transaction; create another handle for another concurrent transaction. A typical authorization path calls pam_authenticate, optionally pam_setcred, then pam_acct_mgmt; it calls pam_open_session before granting a session and pam_close_session while tearing it down. Password changes use pam_chauthtok. Regardless of the path, the application calls pam_end(pamh, last_status), which invalidates the handle and runs registered cleanup callbacks.

item.title: Deploying Grafana
item.description:
Grafana is a visualization and alerting service. A production deployment needs more than a running container: it needs durable state, reproducible provisioning, authenticated access, and a backup and upgrade procedure.

Run Grafana with Persistent State #

Grafana stores users, dashboards created in the UI, alerting data, and configuration metadata in its database. For a small installation, persist the default SQLite database; for highly available deployments, use a supported external database and run multiple Grafana instances behind a load balancer.

item.title: Cryptography Standards and Encodings
item.description:
Cryptographic names often identify an issuing organization and a document series. A protocol must name the exact version, algorithm identifiers, parameters, and encoding rules it implements; a broad label such as “PKCS” or “X.509” is insufficient.

ITU-T X-Series and X.509 #

The ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector (ITU-T) publishes Recommendations in lettered series. The X-series covers data networks, open systems communications, and security. ITU-T X.509 defines a public-key certificate framework and an ASN.1 certificate structure. The IETF profiles X.509 certificates for Internet use in RFC 5280.

It can cache static assets and, depending on the provider, proxy dynamic traffic, terminate TLS, filter attacks, and optimize connections. The origin remains the authoritative application; the CDN is an intermediary with an explicit caching and routing policy.

Connect a Domain to a CDN #

Linkage determines whether declarations in different scopes or translation units denote the same entity, while storage duration determines how long an object exists. Keeping those four questions separate makes dense C and C++ declarations easier to reason about.

item.title: Linux Kernel Infrastructure
item.description:
Subsystem code depends on infrastructure spread across generic headers, architecture overrides, generated files, and core implementation directories. The following notes organize several mechanisms that do not belong to one device or protocol subsystem: diagnostics, error-valued pointers, branch hints and patchable branches, one-copy accesses, and SLUB allocation paths.

Diagnostics and Error Reporting #

Kernel diagnostics use severity-specific pr_*() macros and device-aware dev_*() macros:

c 
if (revision < minimum_revision) {
 dev_err(dev, "unsupported revision %#x\n", revision);
 return -ENODEV;
}

pr_debug("queue depth: %u\n", depth);

dev_err() includes device context; pr_err() is appropriate when no device exists. Dynamic debug can enable selected pr_debug() and dev_dbg() call sites without promoting permanent log noise. Rate-limited variants such as pr_warn_ratelimited() protect the log from recurring conditions.

item.title: ARM Architecture Introduction
item.description:
Arm defines a family of instruction set architectures (ISAs), not one processor implementation. The architecture specifies programmer-visible state, instruction semantics, exceptions, privilege, and memory ordering. A core’s pipeline, cache hierarchy, and branch predictor are microarchitectural choices.

Architecture profiles separate deployment requirements. A-profile targets application processors with virtual memory, R-profile targets real-time systems, and M-profile targets microcontrollers. The execution states and privilege model below describe A-profile systems unless stated otherwise.

Execution States and Instruction Sets #

AArch32 provides 32-bit general-purpose registers and can execute the A32 instruction set or the variable-length T32 instruction set historically called Thumb. AArch64, introduced by Armv8-A, provides thirty-one 64-bit general-purpose registers and the fixed-width A64 instruction set. X0 through X30 name the 64-bit registers; W0 through W30 name their low 32 bits. Writing a W register clears the upper half of its corresponding X register.

item.title: DNS Wire Format
item.description:
DNS queries and responses begin with a 12-byte header followed by Question, Answer, Authority, and Additional sections. All multi-octet integer fields use network byte order. RFC 1035 defines the base format; EDNS, DNSSEC, and later extensions add records and header semantics without changing the base header.

Header #

Field Bits Purpose
ID 16 Client-selected identifier echoed in the response
QR 1 Query (0) or response (1)
Opcode 4 Operation; QUERY is zero
AA 1 Authoritative answer indicator in responses
TC 1 Message was truncated
RD 1 Client requests recursion
RA 1 Server offers recursion
Z 3 Reserved base bits; extensions use AD and CD
RCODE 4 Base response code
QDCOUNT 16 Question count
ANCOUNT 16 Answer record count
NSCOUNT 16 Authority record count
ARCOUNT 16 Additional record count

RD asks the receiving server to perform recursion; RA advertises that the server can do so. AA says the responding server is authoritative for the answer, not that every record in the message is authoritative. TC tells a client that it must retry over TCP or another supported transport when the truncated response is insufficient.

item.title: Spring Overview and Transactions
item.description:
Spring Framework provides a dependency-injection container plus focused modules for AOP, data access, transactions, messaging, and web applications. Transaction management demonstrates the framework’s integration model: application code declares a boundary, while an interceptor coordinates a resource-specific PlatformTransactionManager or reactive transaction manager.

Proxy-Based Declarative Transactions #

With the default advice mode, Spring wraps an eligible bean in an AOP proxy. Calls entering a method matched by @Transactional pass through TransactionInterceptor, which reads transaction metadata, starts or joins a transaction, invokes the target, and commits or rolls back.

item.title: RSA Encryption and Signatures
item.description: RSA defines trapdoor operations on integers modulo a composite number. Secure systems use those operations only through standardized encryption or signature schemes because textbook RSA is deterministic, malleable, and structurally unsafe.

item.title: GNU Make
item.description:
GNU Make is both a dependency-description language and a text-expansion language. A Makefile first defines a graph of files, prerequisites, and recipes; its variables, functions, conditionals, and directives determine which parts of that graph exist. Make then decides which targets are stale and executes the recipes required to update them.

Keeping these two roles separate while reading a Makefile prevents several common errors. Variable and function expansion can happen while Make reads a rule, while it searches for a rule, or while it executes a recipe. In contrast, a recipe’s shell commands run only after Make has constructed enough of the graph to choose an update plan.

item.title: X.509 Certificates
item.description:
An X.509 certificate binds a subject public key to an asserted subject identity through an issuer signature. Certificate validation determines whether that binding is acceptable for a specific protocol and connection. Parsing a certificate or verifying its signature alone is not sufficient.

Encoding and Certificate Structure #

Certificates are ASN.1 values conventionally encoded with DER. PEM is the base64 text form of a DER object:

text 
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

The signed tbsCertificate contains a version, issuer-unique serial number, issuer distinguished name, validity interval, subject distinguished name, SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI), and extensions. The outer certificate also contains the issuer’s signature algorithm identifier and signature over tbsCertificate. The issuer public key is not embedded as a separate certificate field; it is found by constructing a path to an issuer certificate or trust anchor.

item.title: Unix compress and LZW
item.description:
The historical Unix compress utility writes files conventionally named .Z. It uses an LZW-family dictionary coder, not DEFLATE. uncompress and zcat expose compatible command-line interfaces on systems that ship the format.

LZW Initialization and Synchronization #

An LZW encoder starts with entries for the single-byte alphabet. It keeps a current phrase w, reads the next byte k, and continues while w + k is in the dictionary. When that phrase is absent, it emits the code for w, adds w + k, and starts with k. A decoder emits the string for each code and, after the first code, adds the previous decoded string plus the first byte of the current string. After input is exhausted, the encoder emits its final phrase. The encoder and decoder therefore add the same entries one code behind.

item.title: AUR Package Dependencies
item.description:
An AUR repository supplies a PKGBUILD: executable packaging metadata, not a binary package or a dependency resolver. Building a package safely therefore requires distinguishing the dependencies that make the build possible from the dependencies installed on the resulting system.

Dependency Classes in PKGBUILD #

PKGBUILD(5) defines dependency arrays with different lifetimes:

  • depends declares packages required to run the installed package.
  • makedepends declares tools and libraries required only while building.
  • checkdepends declares packages needed by check().

Version constraints use pacman’s dependency syntax, for example depends=('libfoo>=2'). Split packages can have package-specific dependency arrays such as package_client() { depends=('libclient') }.

item.title: Grizzly HTTP Server
item.description:
Grizzly is a Java NIO networking framework maintained by the Eclipse EE4J project. Its grizzly-framework module builds on Java’s non-blocking I/O APIs; it is not a direct wrapper around a particular operating-system API such as epoll.

Modules #

Common Grizzly modules include:

  • grizzly-http, which provides HTTP protocol support;
  • grizzly-http-server, an embeddable HTTP server with Grizzly’s own API; and
  • grizzly-http-servlet, which provides servlet-related integration.

Grizzly is used by GlassFish and can also run small embedded services. It is an HTTP server, not a Jakarta REST implementation. Combine it with Jersey when serving JAX-RS resources.

item.title: Java Launcher Options
item.description:
The java launcher starts a JVM implementation; many flags are HotSpot implementation options rather than Java language or JVM specification requirements. Use the launcher documentation for the JDK release deployed by the application, because availability and defaults change between releases.

Option Families #

Standard options include --class-path, --module-path, -Dname=value, and -version. HotSpot uses -X for nonstandard options and -XX: for diagnostic and advanced flags. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prepends options to every launcher invocation in its environment, so reserve it for controlled runtime environments and inspect it when a process has unexpected behavior.

item.title: C++ Template Specialization
item.description:
Specialization supplies a definition for a particular template argument list or, for class and variable templates, for a more specific argument pattern. Select specialization only when type-based dispatch is the appropriate interface; use ordinary overloads for function-specific dispatch and concepts for behavioral eligibility.

Full Specializations #

A full specialization names every argument and begins with template <>. Function, class, and variable templates can be fully specialized.

cpp 
template <class T>
struct formatter {
 static const char* name() { return "other"; }
};

template <>
struct formatter<int> {
 static const char* name() { return "int"; }
};

A full specialization is an independent entity. It does not inherit members, definitions, or default template arguments from the primary template; define everything it needs. Declare a full specialization before the first use that would otherwise implicitly instantiate that specialization in every translation unit that uses it.

item.title: Java Generics
item.description:
Java generics provide compile-time type checking while preserving compatibility with pre-generics bytecode. The compiler erases type arguments, inserts casts where required, and may generate bridge methods to preserve overriding after erasure. Consequently List<String> and List<Integer> have the same runtime class, and generic type arguments cannot reliably be recovered from an object.

Invariance and Bounds #

Generic classes are invariant: List<Integer> is not a List<Number>, because the latter would permit inserting a Double. Wildcards express variance at an API boundary.

item.title: JVM Garbage Collection
item.description:
The JVM Specification requires automatic storage management but does not prescribe a collector or heap layout. Collector behavior is therefore a property of the deployed JVM, release, flags, heap size, and workload.

Reachability and Memory Pools #

Tracing begins from GC roots, including live thread stacks and registers, static fields, JNI handles, and VM runtime structures. An object strongly reachable from a root remains live. Soft references may be cleared under memory pressure, weak references do not retain their referents, and phantom references support post-mortem coordination through ReferenceQueue. None is a substitute for deterministic resource cleanup; use try-with-resources and Cleaner only as a safety net. Finalization is deprecated for removal.

item.title: NASM for x86 and x86-64
item.description:
NASM translates Intel-syntax x86 assembly into a flat binary or an object file. A flat binary contains emitted bytes with no standard relocation or symbol metadata. An object file such as ELF, Mach-O, or COFF retains sections, symbols, and relocations so a linker can combine it with other objects and libraries.

Sections, Labels, and Symbols #

An object-file source normally separates executable code, initialized data, and zero-initialized storage:

nasm 
global add_one
extern external_value

section .text
add_one:
 mov eax, edi
 add eax, 1
 ret

section .rodata
message: db "hello", 10
message_size equ $ - message

section .bss
scratch: resq 8

A label defines the current assembly position. GLOBAL exports a symbol to the linker, while EXTERN declares a symbol that another object must define. Local labels beginning with . are scoped to the preceding non-local label. Section names and attributes depend on the output format; .text, .rodata, .data, and .bss are ELF conventions rather than universal NASM keywords.

item.title: Relational Data Modeling
item.description:
An entity-relationship model identifies entity types, their attributes, and relationships before choosing tables. A relational schema then represents each fact once at a defined grain. For example, order_line represents one product on one order, whereas order represents the order header.

Entities, Keys, and Relationships #

Every table needs a candidate key that uniquely identifies its rows. Choose a primary key that is stable, non-null, and suitable for joins. A surrogate key does not remove the need for unique constraints over natural business identities, such as an account’s external identifier.

item.title: Linux TUN/TAP
item.description:
TUN/TAP creates virtual network interfaces connected to a userspace file descriptor. A TUN device carries layer-3 IP packets; a TAP device carries layer-2 Ethernet frames. They are used by VPNs, packet analyzers, userspace network stacks, and virtual machines.

Creating an Interface #

Open /dev/net/tun read-write and issue TUNSETIFF with an ifreq. Set IFF_TUN or IFF_TAP; add IFF_NO_PI when the program should receive only packets or frames. Without IFF_NO_PI, each read starts with a four-byte packet-information header containing flags and protocol. The kernel creates the network interface, after which ip link, ip address, and ip route configure its administrative state, addresses, and routes.

item.title: Bash
item.description:
Bash is both an interactive command language and a scripting runtime. Reliable shell code treats words, exit statuses, and file descriptors as distinct data flows. Start scripts with an explicit interpreter when Bash features are required:

bash 
#!/usr/bin/env bash

bash -c 'commands' name arg1 assigns name to $0 and arg1 to $1. That detail matters when a command string consumes positional parameters.

Shell Grammar and Execution #

A list joins pipelines with ;, &, &&, or ||. && and || are short-circuit operators; & starts an asynchronous list. A pipeline joins commands with |, or with |& when the left command’s standard error is also sent to the pipe.
